title: Patient health records
brief: A hospital network keeps patient charts, orders, notes and scanned documents for 40 hospitals. Doctors need a chart in under a second, no saved note may be lost when a server or a building fails (in a whole-region disaster, at most the last minute of edits may need re-entering from the ward), and an auditor can walk in any day and ask you to prove who looked at what.

clarify.q: What happens if the system is down?
clarify.a: Staff fall back to paper, which is slow and risky. The target is 99.9 percent, about 45 minutes of downtime a month at most (approx.).

clarify.q: Who is allowed to see a chart?
clarify.a: Only staff involved in that patient's care, and every look is written to a log nobody can edit.

clarify.q: Can a copy of the records be kept in a second region?
clarify.a: Yes, under the same privacy contract. That is what makes a regional disaster survivable.
X-ray images and signed forms. They are big and rarely change.

notes: Records are kept for at least 7 years, approx.
Sensitive fields are stored apart from the chart.

Scored data retention: at least 2555 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.

numbers.label: Scan storage kept
numbers.how: 3M patients × about 40 MB of scans each, approx.

hints: Three things are asked of you besides speed: prove access, protect keys, survive a lost region. Which elements give each one?
Compliance checks look for an audit log, a key service, a privacy vault, backups and an identity provider. Connect servers to all of them.
The regional recovery point is distinct from building durability and must be verifiable. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Records are a correctness and proof problem more than a speed problem. The traffic is moderate; the hard parts are the audit, the leaked key and the lost region. Each has a dedicated element, and the design is mostly about connecting them.

designs.name: Proof built in, second region running hot
designs.why: A WAF guards the front, an identity provider ties every action to a person, and the audit log taps every server. Keys sit in a key service so a leak can be fixed by rotating them. The database has two zones and synchronous copies, and a second region runs active-active, so it takes over in about a minute. It costs about as much as the main system again; a warm standby at about 40 percent would take about 15 minutes, too long for this uptime target.

tradeoffs: Active-active costs about 100 percent of the main system again and recovers in about a minute. A warm standby costs about 40 percent and takes about 15 minutes; backup-and-restore is far cheaper and takes hours (approx.).
The privacy vault (about $1,000 a month) is a fixed price you pay once, whatever the traffic, to keep sensitive fields in one controlled place.
Key rotation and an audit log do not make traffic faster. They make a bad day short and provable.
Scans in object storage cost a fraction of database storage, but a scan is fetched in a second request after the chart.
editorial.realWorld: Hospital record systems are often expected to be up 99.9 to 99.99 percent of the time, and health law in many countries requires access logs and encryption. A 120 TB archive of scans is about $2,800 a month in standard object storage (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Patient health records: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Acknowledge durable clinical edits and retain auditable access across recovery. The stated loss boundary determines which failure domains must persist before acknowledgement. Avoiding lost clinical edits requires concurrency control, not just replication. The regional recovery point is distinct from building durability and must be verifiable.

fields.label: Step 1. A doctor saves note N before a building fails. What permits acknowledgement?
options: A durable copy beyond that building plus the note version and edit id
fields.explanation: The stated loss boundary determines which failure domains must persist before acknowledgement.

fields.label: Step 2. Two doctors edit N from the same old version. What happens?
options: Detect the version conflict and preserve both edits for merge or review
Silently overwrite whichever save arrived first
fields.explanation: Avoiding lost clinical edits requires concurrency control, not just replication.

fields.label: Step 3. A regional recovery loses the last 40 seconds of edits. What is required?
options: Claim zero loss because replication was enabled
A measured recovery gap within one minute, re-entry workflow and access audit continuity
fields.explanation: The regional recovery point is distinct from building durability and must be verifiable.

correctness.responsibility: Acknowledge durable clinical edits and retain auditable access across recovery.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 750 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $21126. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
